item.title: The integrable Lie-Trotter-Suzuki decomposition for nonlinear dynamics: Efficient Hamiltonian simulation of the Stepanoff flow
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Unitary simulation of non-integrable dynamics via integrable Lie-Trotter-Suzuki decomposition yields explicit tensor product structures with gate complexity 𝒪(δdata−1CQHS) for observable amplitude estimation.

Grade 0.406 · 3.1σ above the day's baseline · matched “Probing many-body dynamics on a 51-atom quantum simulator” · Ilon Joseph, Ivan Novikau, Michael R. Montgomery, Joanna Slawinska, Dimitrios Giannakis

Figure

Measured probability distribution of observables Q~1 and Q~2 from the amplitude estimation quantum circuit compared to exact classical values (black vertical lines) across different precision ancilla counts ny.

Asks

How can the unitary Koopman–von Neumann evolution operator for nonlinear dynamical systems be simulated efficiently without iterative nonlinear operations or dissipative finite-difference terms?

Before

Finite-difference/finite-element representations for the advection equation suffer from poor numerical properties unless dissipation is added; standard Pauli encodings exhibit exponential gate scaling with qubit count.

But

Simulated using a classical emulator of fault-tolerant quantum computers. Courant–Friedrichs–Lewy (CFL) condition forces linear scaling of the time step count with spatial grid resolution N.

Tools

Integrable Lie-Trotter-Suzuki (I-LTS) decomposition · Quantum Signal Processing (QSP) · Quantum Singular Value Transformation (QSVT) · Quantum Fourier Transform (QFT) · QuCF emulator / QuEST toolkit

Abstract

We propose an efficient unitary numerical time integration strategy for nonlinear dynamical systems: the integrable Lie-Trotter-Suzuki decomposition (I-LTS). First, express the generator as a sum of integrable parts. Second, approximate the full evolution operator using a Lie-Trotter-Suzuki (LTS) decomposition of the desired approximation order in time step. The I-LTS construction ensures that the full evolution operator can be represented as a product of terms that each have an efficient explicit tensor product factorization that can be handled efficiently with tensor network and/or quantum block-encoding methods. Next, we apply this method to an important non-integrable point example of a dynamical system: the Stepanoff flow on the torus. First, we derive an efficient unitary quantum algorithm for simulating the Stepanoff flow that can be thought of as a unitary classical version of a quantum map. Then, we provide a detailed description of the encoding of the two-dimensional system into an efficient quantum circuit, including an efficient block-encoding for all required operators. An efficient Hamiltonian simulation algorithm is constructed using a sequence of alternating quantum Fourier transforms (QFT) and Quantum Signal Processing (QSP) circuits. Finally, the circuit is simulated using a numerical emulator of fault-tolerant quantum computers, and the results are found to be consistent with several alternative classical computational methods. While efficient, the need for Trotterization introduces fundamental complexity in requiring small enough time step for an accurate approximation and solving for the transfer operator requires one to confront the linear scaling of the advection operator with grid size.

item.title: Estimating the Trotter error via phase analysis
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Trotter operator-distance error approximates as τ2‖Φˆ2‖ for small step size τ, where ‖Φˆ2‖=12‖∑p1∑p2<p1[Hˆp1,Hˆp2]‖. This expression upper bounds the error per step at large step counts s due to destructive interference across steps.

Grade 0.406 · 3.1σ above the day's baseline · matched “Theory of Trotter Error with Commutator Scaling” · Maxime Dion, Benjamin D'Anjou

Figure

Rescaled Trotter error η versus dimensionless step size ‖Hˆ‖τ across multiple random Hamiltonians. Exact error tracks close to η=0 (the proposed phase operator estimate ‖Φˆ2‖τ2) rather than the standard upper bound η=1.

Asks

Why are general operator-distance Trotter error bounds excessively loose in practice, and how can the actual error be estimated more tightly?

Before

Childs et al. (2021) general operator-norm bound prefactor α1=12∑p1‖∑p2<p1[Hˆp1,Hˆp2]‖, which applies the triangle inequality over outer sums and overestimates error for Hamiltonians with more than two noncommuting terms.

But

Small Trotter step size τ regime; finite-dimensional Hilbert spaces; unperturbed unitary evolution without physical noise.

Tools

Hermitian phase operator formalism · BCH / Magnus-type expansion in nested commutators · Adjoint representation sinc filtering

Abstract

Good Trotter error estimates are crucial to correctly assess the resources required to perform an approximate time evolution with a target accuracy. General bounds for finite-size quantum systems are found to be very loose in practice, and it is therefore highly desirable to improve on them. In this work, we analyze the Trotter error in terms of the spectrum of a phase operator that we construct from the Hamiltonian. In the limit of a small Trotter step size, we obtain an estimate of the Trotter error written in terms of a sum of nested commutators between terms of the Hamiltonian. The structure of this estimate allows us to naturally explain the looseness of general bounds. We show that even for a finite step size, our estimate typically remains more accurate than general bounds. Moreover, we argue that it becomes an upper bound for the Trotter error per step in the limit of a large number of steps, reflecting the destructive interference of the errors across steps. Our results provide useful practical heuristics for resource optimization in quantum simulations.

item.title: Quditology: harnessing many levels for quantum information processing
item.description:
Pay dirt review — Survey of qudit quantum information hardware demonstrates that multi-level d>2 architectures match the Hilbert space of 70 qubits using 24 qudits with d=8, achieving gate-depth reductions exceeding one order of magnitude in dedicated quantum simulations.

Grade 0.403 · 3.0σ above the day's baseline · matched “Evidence for the utility of quantum computing before fault tolerance” · Abhijit Chakraborty, Zheng Shi, Noah Goss, Irfan Siddiqi, Barry C. Sanders, Christine A. Muschik

Figure

Landscape of qudit implementations showing controllable qudit dimension d on the horizontal axis versus the number of interacting qudits n on the vertical axis across experimental platforms.

Asks

What is the current experimental state of the art in high-fidelity state preparation, control, measurement, and fault tolerance across diverse qudit platforms?

But

Increased spectral crowding, heightened sensitivity to phase decoherence, energy relaxation across higher levels, and elevated classical and quantum crosstalk.

Tools

trapped ions · superconducting circuits · solid-state nuclear spins · photonic circuits · neutral atoms

Abstract

Quantum computing offers the prospect of surpassing classical computation on certain tasks by leveraging quantum coherence and entanglement. However, a significant gap remains between current quantum hardware and the requirements to transcend what classical computers can achieve, with decoherence limiting the capacity of storing quantum information and the number of logical steps that can be executed reliably. In the long term, fault tolerance bridges this gap, but simply changing the numerical base from binary to higher base d is a viable way to 'squeeze more juice'---get more quantum information processing---from a quantum computer of given size. Additionally, for quantum simulations, qudits offer a natural encoding scheme for high-dimensional physical degrees of freedom. Here, we review recent experimental progress in high-fidelity preparation, control, and measurement of qudits across various platforms such as trapped ions, superconducting circuits, solid-state nuclear spins, photonic systems, and neutral atoms. We highlight early demonstrations of qudit-based quantum simulation, computation and error suppression enabled by these developments, heralding the transition of qudits from conceptual constructs to viable building blocks for quantum technologies. Finally, we outline key challenges and potential future directions for scalable qudit quantum information processing.

item.title: A Path Integral Method with Far-Field Expansion for Open Quantum Dynamics
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Hybridizing QuAPI's exponential near-field bath influence across r time steps with a FRODS-type far-field Taylor expansion yields O(Δt2) global accuracy. At β=5 and ξ=0.75, maximum spin-boson error drops from 0.0607 (FRODS) to 0.032 (r=0) and 0.00031 (r=3).

Grade 0.382 · 2.7σ above the day's baseline · matched “Probing many-body dynamics on a 51-atom quantum simulator” · Zhenning Cai

Figure

Population difference ⟨σz(t)⟩ as a function of time t across four temperatures β∈{5,2,1,0.5}, comparing FRODS and PIFFE for r=0,1,2,3 against benchmark QuAPI.

Asks

Can QuAPI and FRODS be unified into a deterministic path integral method that bypasses QuAPI's exponential memory scaling without suffering FRODS's accuracy loss at practical step sizes and strong bath couplings?

Before

FRODS had maximum deviation against QuAPI of 0.0607 at β=5, 0.0674 at β=2, and 0.0723 at β=0.5 (for ξ=0.75, Δt=0.125).

But

Deterministic Gaussian harmonic bath linearly and diagonally coupled to the system; fixed memory cutoff Kmax⁡ and auxiliary degree cutoff Dmax⁡.

Tools

path integral method with far-field expansion (PIFFE) · Feynman-Vernon influence functional · symmetric second-order Trotter splitting · auxiliary degree truncation

Abstract

We establish a connection between the quasi-adiabatic propagator path integral (QuAPI) method and fast resummation of Dyson series (FRODS). Building on this connection, we introduce a path integral method with far-field expansion (PIFFE) for quantum systems coupled linearly to a thermal Gaussian bath. PIFFE combines QuAPI with a Taylor expansion of the far-field bath influence, keeping interactions within r time steps in exponential form. The scheme has error O(Δt²) at fixed final time and is free of stochastic or tensor-compression errors. Spin-boson tests show that PIFFE gives results much closer to QuAPI than FRODS does, even for small r, while requiring substantially less storage than QuAPI. This allows much longer bath memory lengths and simulations of multilevel systems. Truncating the bath memory and limiting the total auxiliary degree further reduce storage and computational costs.

item.title: Unified preparation of exact and asymptotic quantum many-body scars from Dicke states
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Unified quantum algorithm prepares exact and asymptotic quantum many-body scars from Dicke states via block encoding and isometries. Success probability has a strictly positive lower bound independent of system size M and scar index n at fixed target fidelity.

Grade 0.380 · 2.6σ above the day's baseline · matched “Probing many-body dynamics on a 51-atom quantum simulator” · Yuki Asari, Masaya Kunimi, Tetsuro Nikuni

Figure

Energy variance ΔE2/J2 versus system size M for the algorithm output and ideal states of the spin-1 XY model, alongside time-dependent self-overlap fidelity under depolarizing gate noise.

Asks

Can asymptotic and exact quantum many-body scar states across different nonintegrable models be prepared systematically on digital quantum simulators?

But

Numerical verification up to M=12 spins under depolarizing gate noise (ε1∼10−4,ε2∼1.5×10−3). Tested specifically on spin-1 XY, domain-wall-conserving, and Onsager scar models with open boundary conditions.

Tools

block encoding · amplitude amplification (Grover iteration) · isometry mapping · Bärtschi–Eidenbenz Dicke state preparation · noisy quantum trajectory simulations

Abstract

We propose a unified quantum algorithm for preparing exact and asymptotic quantum many-body scar (QMBS) states in the spin-1 XY, domain-wall-conserving, and Onsager scar models. Model-dependent isometries map the exact scar states to Dicke states and the target asymptotic QMBS states to gapless magnon excitations of the spin-1/2 ferromagnetic Heisenberg chain. Exact QMBS states are prepared by applying the inverse isometries to Dicke states. For asymptotic QMBS states, block encoding first prepares the magnon excitations from Dicke states to a prescribed fidelity, after which the inverse isometries map the prepared states back to the physical chains. At fixed target fidelity, the block-encoding success probability has a positive lower bound independent of system size and scar index, implying that a constant number of amplitude amplification rounds suffices. Our algorithm enables systematic studies of nonergodic dynamics on programmable quantum simulators.

item.title: Quantum Algorithm for Direct Estimation of Energy-Level Differences via Quantum Dynamics Simulation
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Estimates energy-level differences ΔE directly via Hadamard test combining H(λ) and H(λ+δλ) time evolutions. Decouples sampling complexity from the full Hamiltonian operator norm ‖H‖, scaling instead with parameter shift δλ and the derivative operator norm.

Grade 0.378 · 2.6σ above the day's baseline · matched “Evidence for the utility of quantum computing before fault tolerance” · Norifumi Matsumoto, Yuya O. Nakagawa, Shota Kanasugi, Yuichiro Hidaka, Kazunori Maruyama, Hirotaka Oshima

Figure

Overview of hybrid workflow: quantum circuit runs a modified Hadamard test with H(λ) and H(λ+δλ) evolutions, feeding measurement statistics to classical processing to output ΔE.

Asks

How to estimate minute energy-level differences and gradients without the sampling complexity scaling with the full Hamiltonian operator norm?

Before

Statistical phase estimation estimates energies separately, requiring sampling cost scaling with the full Hamiltonian operator norm ‖H‖ that grows with system size.

But

Early fault-tolerant quantum computing setting, assumes initial state overlap with target state, perturbative shift regime.

Tools

Hadamard test circuit · statistical phase estimation · non-adaptive classical reconstruction · spectral cumulative distribution function

Abstract

We present a quantum algorithm for the early fault-tolerant quantum computing (early-FTQC) era that estimates minute energy-level differences, such as energy gradients and molecular forces, at a lower sampling cost than existing phase-estimation methods. Such energy derivatives, accessed as the small energy difference induced by an infinitesimal parameter shift, are central to quantum simulation in chemistry and materials science. Although Statistical Phase Estimation (SPE) is well-suited to energy estimation in this era, applying it to an energy difference demands a sampling complexity that scales with the operator norm of the full Hamiltonian, which grows with system size. Our algorithm overcomes this by incorporating two time-evolution operators, corresponding to the Hamiltonians before and after the parameter shift, into a single quantum circuit, which is combined with a non-adaptive, statistically sampled reconstruction in the energy-difference domain. This reduces the relevant scale from the operator norm of the full Hamiltonian to that of the operator norm of the Hamiltonian derivative and the parameter shift, thereby lowering the sampling complexity. We further propose the joint estimation of energy eigenvalues and their differences, giving a holistic view of the energy landscape. Numerical simulations and resource estimations on prototypical systems, such as the Fermi-Hubbard model, demonstrate the resulting reductions in required resources without compromising precision. This positions energy-difference estimation as a practical task for early-FTQC devices, opening a route to molecular forces, response properties, and excited-state energy differences.

item.arxave:abstract: We present a quantum algorithm for the early fault-tolerant quantum computing (early-FTQC) era that estimates minute energy-level differences, such as energy gradients and molecular forces, at a lower sampling cost than existing phase-estimation methods. Such energy derivatives, accessed as the small energy difference induced by an infinitesimal parameter shift, are central to quantum simulation in chemistry and materials science. Although Statistical Phase Estimation (SPE) is well-suited to energy estimation in this era, applying it to an energy difference demands a sampling complexity that scales with the operator norm of the full Hamiltonian, which grows with system size. Our algorithm overcomes this by incorporating two time-evolution operators, corresponding to the Hamiltonians before and after the parameter shift, into a single quantum circuit, which is combined with a non-adaptive, statistically sampled reconstruction in the energy-difference domain. This reduces the relevant scale from the operator norm of the full Hamiltonian to that of the operator norm of the Hamiltonian derivative and the parameter shift, thereby lowering the sampling complexity. We further propose the joint estimation of energy eigenvalues and their differences, giving a holistic view of the energy landscape. Numerical simulations and resource estimations on prototypical systems, such as the Fermi-Hubbard model, demonstrate the resulting reductions in required resources without compromising precision. This positions energy-difference estimation as a practical task for early-FTQC devices, opening a route to molecular forces, response properties, and excited-state energy differences.

item.title: TyxonQ: A Workflow Layer for Quantum Computing in Chemistry
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Presents TyxonQ, a multiscale chemistry workflow layer unifying four hand-off interfaces linking classical simulation (ASE, i-PI, OpenMM, LAMMPS, MDI), embedding, variational/sampling quantum solvers, and execution backends via a shared energy/force scanner contract.

Grade 0.354 · 2.2σ above the day's baseline · matched “Probing many-body dynamics on a 51-atom quantum simulator” · Xiaoran Li, Zhi Yin, Zhupeng Han, Zhengquan Pan, Kangyu Zheng

Figure

Architecture of the four multiscale workflow hand-offs (H1–H4), illustrating how classical molecular mechanics, conventional electronic structure, active-space quantum solvers, and classical trajectory consumers interact through unified interfaces.

Asks

How can quantum chemistry solvers and fragment embedding be connected into existing multiscale classical molecular mechanics and dynamics workflows across consistent energy and gradient interfaces?

But

Demonstrations use local numerical evaluation, state-vector simulation, or zero-shot configuration rather than physical hardware execution. Gradient workflows are limited to small test systems (H2, LiH, H2O) and executed consumer validation is ASE geometry optimization rather than full MD trajectories.

Tools

TyxonQ 1.4.0 · PySCF · energy and nuclear force scanners (QCScanner) · embedded wavefunction (EWF) / QM/MM adapters · ASE / i-PI / OpenMM / MDI consumers

Code. https://github.com/QureGenAI-Biotech/TyxonQ

Abstract

Quantum computational chemistry is often framed around a hybrid quantum solver. In practical applications, however, bottlenecks to adoption also lie in the surrounding multiscale workflow. A molecular problem may combine classical molecular mechanics and dynamics, conventional electronic-structure calculations, and a quantum solver for selected orbitals or embedded fragments. This division of work is particularly relevant when a chemically important electronic subspace is strongly correlated. The size of the electronic Hilbert space and the qubit, noise, and circuit-depth constraints of noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) devices make active-space and embedding choices central to a feasible quantum calculation. The resulting energies and gradients must remain consistent with the surrounding classical simulation. We present TyxonQ, a workflow layer that connects these levels of treatment rather than addressing only the hybrid quantum algorithm. Four integration interfaces link PySCF-compatible energy/force scanners and embedding, solver adapters, simulator and hardware backends, and classical consumers. The implementation combines QM/MM and fragment embedding with conventional CCSD/FCI fragment solvers, variational and sampling-based quantum methods, and adapters for ASE, i-PI, OpenMM, LAMMPS (through i-PI), and MDI. We describe the contracts and audit coverage, and evaluate correctness, switching cost, reproducibility, and artifact portability on small chemistry workflows, distinguishing executed paths from source-level support. The purpose of TyxonQ is to support incremental integration of quantum calculations into existing computational chemistry workflows, including those used in industry, while retaining appropriate classical treatments elsewhere.

item.title: A novel quantum lattice Boltzmann methodology for cosmological radiation transport
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Angular redistribution step eliminates directional ray anisotropy for point sources in quantum lattice Boltzmann simulations. Crossing beam tests on D2Q8 grids up to 16×16 show zero unphysical collisions, zero beam-width dispersion, and constant intensity through crossings.

Grade 0.334 · 1.8σ above the day's baseline · matched “Simulating physics with computers” · Rasmit Devkota, John Wise

Figure

Intensity profiles (top) and fractional error (bottom) on a 16×8 grid across 3, 4, and 5 light-crossing times. Two 45-degree beams pass through each other under periodic boundaries without collision artifacts or spreading, with error dropping near beam intersections due to central-limit sampling effects.

Asks

How can quantum lattice Boltzmann algorithms be adapted to accurately simulate non-scattering radiative transfer from point sources in two and three dimensions?

Before

Existing 1D and planar 2D quantum lattice Boltzmann radiative transfer schemes (Farhadinia and Succi, 2024) rely on scattering media and produce severe ray anisotropy for localized point sources in non-scattering cosmological media.

But

Simulated on classical hardware/ideal state simulators rather than real quantum processors; non-relativistic regime only; redistributing radiation introduces artificial dispersion that weakens sharp shadows behind absorbing clouds.

Tools

Quantum Lattice Boltzmann Method (QLBM) · D2Q4 and D2Q8 discrete velocity schemes · Householder reflection angular redistribution operator · Qiskit simulator

Abstract

Radiation transport is an essential process in many physical simulations, including cosmological codes which track stellar and diffuse radiation. Many present codes utilize ray tracing or moment methods, but these grow increasingly difficult and expensive for large simulations. Quantum lattice Boltzmann methods exponentially reduce complexity by propagating radiation over a lattice, allowing for better spatial resolution without needing to introduce adaptive ray tracing or other optimizations. However, existing formulations result in poor angular resolution for radiation point sources. In this work, we propose an angular redistribution methodology which significantly improves the resolution with minimal increase in complexity. We verify the correctness of the method on both classical processors and quantum simulators and outline how the quantum algorithm can be integrated into existing codes. This method is an important step towards fully-quantum radiation hydrodynamics simulation which could exponentially accelerate existing cosmological codes, enabling simulations at scales currently infeasible.
